title: Inter-sku Driver Epochal Stability Journal
content:
Purpose:
This is a running lab journal documenting an experiment series to capture 'epochal' (time‑bounded) stability regressions introduced by driver and CUDA updates across cloud SKUs (A100/H100/L40S variants). Goal is to produce reproducible diffs that help us: 1) attribute regressions to driver/CUDA/firmware, 2) propose mitigations (fallback kernels, pinning policies), and 3) produce a compact report for SRE/Release teams.

Context / motivation:
- We keep seeing transient small-to-medium p99 jumps after cloud providers roll drivers or CUDA on host images. These are often not reproduced in single-point synthetic tests. Suspect interaction of: kernel launch rate, NVLINK/PCIE path mode, host CPU governor, and low-level driver micro-updates.
- This journal focuses on cross-sku *epochal* comparisons: run identical workload across three consecutive driver/CUDA epochs and record micro-profiles, kernel histograms, and decode throughput.

Scope & constraints:
- SKUs: AWS p4dn (A100), GCP a2-highgpu (A100), AWS hpc instances (H100), Azure HBv3-like (L40S equivalent). Try to match RAM/CPU where possible but not strict.
- Driver/CUDA epochs: pick three consecutive driver builds from each provider (example: nvidia-driver-525.x -> 535.x -> 545.x; CUDA 11.8 -> 12.0 -> 12.2) where available.
- Models: a small-medium decoder (7B) and a long-context 13B decode (to stress KV caching and memory).
- Workload: steady token stream generator with synthetic mix: 30% long prompts (2k), 70% short (64). Target qps to exercise tail-latency and kernel-launch frequency (configurable 8–32 concurrent requests).
- Telemetry: per-token latency, kernel-launch rate, cudaMemcpy ops, NVLINK errors, GPU power, SM utilization, PCIe error counters, and eBPF traces on host for kernel scheduling.

Experiment plan (high level):
1) Baseline: pick an epoch-old image that we last validated (call it E0). Run controlled job for 8h, collect full traces.
2) Upgrade driver/CUDA to E1 on same instance type and repeat identical run immediately after a fresh boot.
3) Repeat for E2. If cloud automatically applied micro-updates, pin to image snapshots and re-run to capture drift.
4) Repeat the whole sequence across each SKU + region (us-west-2, us-east-1, europe-west1).
5) For any observed p95/p99 regressions, capture a minimized repro: reduce to the smallest QPS/context that triggers it and record the timeline.

Data to capture (per run):
- run_id (timestamp), sku, region, driver_version, cuda_version, kernel_modules list (lsmod output), dmesg tail, nv-smi top snapshot, nvidia-smi --query results (power, mem, sm), perf traces for top 10 CUDA kernels, eBPF host scheduling samples, p50/p95/p99 per-request token latency, decode throughput (tokens/s), KV cache miss ratio, and simple per-kernel latency histograms.

Early findings (notes from initial week of runs):
- A100 (AWS p4dn)
  - Epoch E0 (driver 525/CUDA 11.8) stable baseline: p99 ~ 190ms for short tokens, tail very tight.
  - Epoch E1 (driver 535/CUDA 12.0) introduced sporadic ~2–4x p99 spikes correlated with kernel launch queueing. Kernel histograms show a subpopulation of launches that jump to 6–12ms (normally 0.6–1.2ms).
  - dmesg showed intermittent PCIe link re-training messages during spikes (rare but present).
  - nv-smi logs: transient drop in SM util concurrent with launch latency spikes (possible firmware/driver handshake causing stalls).

- H100 (GCP-like variant)
  - E0 -> E1 upgrade small steady improvement in average throughput but an increase in p95 jitter.
  - eBPF host traces show increased preemption of realtime threads under E1; scheduler config differs (cpu governor / sysctl differences introduced by image). When we manually set rtprio and cpu governor to performance, jitter subsided.
  - Implication: not strictly driver-only; host image/sysctl changes often shipped with CUDA bundles matter.

- L40S-like (Azure)
  - Large context runs (13B long) show memory reclamation patterns that align with driver epoch changes; specific driver introduced a more aggressive gddr refresh cadence -> slight p50 increase but significant p99 tails when sustained decode > 1000 tokens.

Repro tips / gotchas observed:
- Reproducing tails is time-sensitive: if you run after node boot vs ~30m uptime you can see different kernel cache warm states. Always run warmup sequence of 20–30 long requests before measurement window.
- Image packages often override /etc/modprobe.d settings (e.g., persistent behavior for nvidia-persistenced). Double-check these after upgrade.
- Some cloud SKUs have automatic host-side driver rollback tooling — ensure that the pinned image actually contains expected driver (we had one run where the image label said 545 but a micro-rollback put 543 on the node).

Example minimized repro (notes):
- SKU: AWS p4dn.xlarge-equivalent
- Driver: 535.54 -> spikes observed
- Workload: 12 concurrent short requests (64 tokens) with 2 long warmups every 60s
- Observed: p99 bursts at 6x baseline approximately every ~7–12 minutes. Captured dmesg showing "pci_bus ... link training" within 3s of spike.
- Mitigation attempted: pinned PCIe ASPM off in modprobe config -> spike frequency reduced but did not disappear.

Hypotheses to test next:
- PCIe link power-management interplay with driver kernel path during rapid kernel launches. Test by toggling ASPM/pstate and measuring kernel launch histogram.
- Driver micro-update changed fallback path for a specific cuBLAS/cuSPARSE kernel causing a rare slow path on certain tensor sizes. Need perf analysis to map slow launches to kernel names.
- Host image sysctl/cpu governor differences are a confounder. Create a minimal image with identical host config across epochs and re-run.

Action items / checklist:
- [ ] Standardize warmup protocol across all runs (scripted). - Owner: Arjun
- [ ] Add kernel-name to our per-kernel histogram exporter (so slow launches can be traced to kernel symbol). - Owner: Elena
- [ ] Create pinned image snapshots for each epoch to avoid auto-rollback drift. - Owner: SRE team (Samir to coordinate)
- [ ] Run isolated PCIe ASPM toggle sweep on A100 and H100 to validate hypothesis. - Owner: Maya
- [ ] Postmortem template: build one-page for each observed regression and link to PR/rollback recommendation. - Owner:release-eng

Open questions / discussion points:
- Can we push a tiny kernel shim that logs kernel launch latencies and attributes them to module/drivers in production? Feels invasive but could be invaluable for root cause.
- How often do cloud providers change host level sysctl defaults when they update CUDA/driver stacks? Need a contact at providers to understand release notes granularity.
- Is there business tolerance for pinning drivers for 30 days vs applying updates quickly? Operational cost vs stability tradeoff.

Quick references / links used in runs:
- internal ticket: JIRA-INF-2147 (driver-epochal-stability)
- PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/4823 (extended telemetry exporter)
- Slack thread: #infra-gpu (thread ts: 1704012345.000200)

Notes-to-self:
- Keep experiment logs in CSV per-run with these columns: run_id, sku, region, driver, cuda, p50, p95, p99, mean_power, sm_util_mean, kernel_slow_count. Put CSVs in /shared/benchmarks/driver-epochal/raw/ for ingestion.
- When summarizing for product (if asked): focus on customer-visible SLO impact and clear rollback thresholds. Engineers want root cause, GTM wants customer-facing mitigation plan.

Appendix: immediate low-effort mitigations to try in next run window:
- enforce performance governor + rtprio for runtime threads
- disable PCIe ASPM via kernel param at boot
- increase nv-persistenced priority to reduce handshake overhead
- instrument kernel-launch histogram by symbol (minimal overhead sampling)

End of journal entry (will append new epochs as they are run).
